# Overview

Data from Antarctic Weather Stations (AWS) is used to reconstruct climate conditions for a hindcast model for a specific region of Antarctica for the purpose of development of a new station base. The data includes temperature, wind speed, and other meteorological variables collected from various AWS locations across the continent.

New station location: 83°48'10.68"S and 146°35'20.85"E

Converts to WGS84 Antarctic Polar Stereographic coordinates: X = 371154.261133, Y = -562545.764708

This data was downloaded from [AMRDC Data Repository](https://amrdcdata.ssec.wisc.edu/dataset/antaws-dataset) on 18/10/2026 and included shapefiles of AWS locations and a dataset of climate variables in different resolutions.

# Setup

Import necessary libraries for data manipulation and visualization.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import geopandas as gpd
from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist
```

## Read in shapefiles

Read in shapefile for Antarctic Weather Stations (AWS) and the base map polygon for Antarctica. 

```{python}
# name shapefiles paths
aws_path = "shapefile/267AWS.shp"
cais_path = "shapefile/CAIS.shp"
polygon_path = "shapefile/cst10_polygon.shp"

# read the shapefiles using geopandas
aws_data = gpd.read_file(aws_path)
cais_data = gpd.read_file(cais_path)
polygon_data = gpd.read_file(polygon_path)

# check data
print(aws_data.head())
print(cais_data.head())
print(polygon_data.head())

# check coordinate reference system
print("Base Map CRS:", polygon_data.crs)
print("Points CRS Before:", aws_data.crs)
print("cais:", cais_data.crs)

# reproject aws station to match base map
points_projected = aws_data.to_crs(polygon_data.crs)

points_projected["geometry"] = points_projected["geometry"].scale(xfact=0.001, yfact=0.001, origin=(0, 0))
polygon_data["geometry"] = polygon_data["geometry"].scale(xfact=0.001, yfact=0.001, origin=(0, 0))
```

# create overall figure and axes

# Calculating Distances Between Stations

Calculate the pairwise distances between all AWS stations using their projected coordinates. This will create a distance matrix that can be used for further analysis.

```{python}
# extract the x and y coordinates of the projected points into a 2D array
XA = np.column_stack((points_projected.geometry.x, points_projected.geometry.y))

# calculate the pairwise Euclidean distance matrix
distance_matrix = cdist(XA, XA, metric='euclidean')

# sense checks!
print(f"Matrix shape: {distance_matrix.shape}") # Output: (N, N)
print(max(distance_matrix.flatten())) # Output: Maximum distance
print(min(distance_matrix.flatten())) # Output: Minimum distance (should be 0)
```


```{python}
# extract labels from your original GeoDataFrame
station_labels = points_projected['zhandian'].tolist()

# wrap the raw cdist matrix in a pandas DataFrame
labeled_matrix = pd.DataFrame(distance_matrix, index=station_labels, columns=station_labels)

# look up specific distances instantly by name
# print(labeled_matrix.loc['Station_A', 'Station_B'])
```


```{python}
## base code if you want to find the most distant stations

# 1. Flatten the grid into rows of point pairs
pairs_df = labeled_matrix.stack().reset_index()
pairs_df.columns = ['Origin', 'Destination', 'Distance']

# 2. Filter out self-matches (where distance is 0)
pairs_df = pairs_df[pairs_df['Origin'] != pairs_df['Destination']]

# 3. Sort by distance descending to see the most distant points at the top
furthest_stations = pairs_df.sort_values(by='Distance', ascending=False)

# Display the top 10 most distant pairs
print(furthest_stations.head(10))

```
